01 — THE STORY

The person behind
the work

Scientist by training, teacher by choice — working where education, honest administration and technology meet.

Based in Buner District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, I completed a BS in Biochemistry at Abdul Wali Khan University Mardan before joining the Elementary & Secondary Education Department as a Primary School Teacher in October 2022. I now teach at Government Primary School Koz Kalay.

Alongside classroom teaching, I serve as my school's focal person for digital work — student profiles, results uploading and EMIS data — where a background in science and technology is put to daily use in public service. Before government service, I spent a year teaching at Fuji Public School, Khanano Dherai: my first classroom, where I learned the craft.

Outside school, my interests run to mobile technology, AI tools, solar energy systems, and learning German — currently at A1 level, one lesson at a time.

"Strong schools are built one honest lesson, one accurate record and one curious child at a time."

RESEARCH

Research & scientific work

From my final-year research at the Department of Biochemistry, AWKUM — a hospital-based study of dengue in Mardan, presented here in full, with its numbers exactly as recorded.

Featured study · Original research manuscript

Demographic, clinical and serological profile of dengue patients admitted to Mardan Medical Complex, Pakistan, October 2019 – January 2020

Shah Fahad · Muhammad Ayaz Khan
Department of Biochemistry, Faculty of Chemical and Life Sciences, Abdul Wali Khan University Mardan, Pakistan · Supervisor: Dr. Sulaiman, Associate Professor
Hospital-based descriptive survey n = 153 admitted patients Oct 2019 – Jan 2020 Manuscript — not published or peer-reviewed
Jump to the Figures
153laboratory-confirmed patients included
72.5%male — 111 men, 42 women
53%of cases admitted in October, the peak month
≈44%knew mosquitoes transmit dengue (68 of 153)

Background. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease spread by Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus. Hospital-based data from district Mardan are scarce.

Methods. Admitted, laboratory-confirmed dengue patients at Mardan Medical Complex were interviewed face to face with a 23-item questionnaire between October 2019 and January 2020. Infection was confirmed by immunochromatographic test (ICT) for NS1 antigen, IgG and IgM. Data were analysed descriptively in Microsoft Excel.

Findings. Of 153 patients, 111 were men (72.5%) and 42 women (27.5%). Most were aged 15–30 years (n=63) or 45–70 years (n=44). Unemployed people (34%) and labourers (25%) predominated, and 69.9% were married. Cases peaked in October (53%). All patients had fever and headache, and all were NS1 positive; 86 were also IgG positive, 29 IgM positive and 38 positive for both. About 44% knew that mosquito bites transmit dengue.

Interpretation. Admitted dengue patients were mainly young and middle-aged men, with a clear post-monsoon peak and low awareness of transmission. Education and vector control should start before autumn. Because this was a hospital-based sample of admitted patients, these findings describe who reached this hospital — they cannot be used to calculate population prevalence or incidence.

Keywords: dengue; Mardan; Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; NS1; IgG; IgM; awareness

Integrity

What this study can — and cannot — claim

A single-centre, hospital-based study of admitted patients over four months. It has no population denominator, so incidence and prevalence cannot be calculated; severity grading, platelet counts and serotypes were not reported; and no inferential statistics were used. Ethics approval details, funding and conflicts of interest are not stated in the paper — details to be confirmed by the author. The full text, discussion and limitations are in the complete study view.

Deployment instructions — putting this site live

This is a single self-contained page: index.html plus the portrait at assets/shah-fahad.jpg. No build step, database or server code is needed — to run it locally, simply open index.html in any browser, or serve the folder with any static file server.

GitHub Pages: push both files (keeping the assets/ folder) to a repository, then enable Pages under Settings → Pages → Deploy from branch. Netlify / Vercel: drag the folder into the deploy dashboard, or connect the repo with no build command and the root as publish directory. Any web host: upload index.html and assets/ via FTP/cPanel to the public folder. Fonts load from the Google Fonts CDN; everything else works offline.

Implemented features: full-screen photo opening (a few seconds, skippable, then gone) · The Knowledge Engine — interactive WebGL 3D with drag, pointer response, static and reduced-motion fallbacks · command-palette navigation (Ctrl/⌘ K) · motion on/off control · hero particle canvas · subtle 3D tilt on portrait and education cards · custom cursor (desktop) · dark/light theme switch · scroll progress bar · active-section navigation · mobile menu · interactive expanding journey timeline · expandable skill panels · live Pakistan-time clock · interactive particle playground · generative-art bloom · three-question knowledge quiz · resume dialog with download · interactive 3D Molecular Universe (DNA, glucose ring/chain, protein ribbon/ball-and-stick/space-filling, honestly labelled illustrative models) · full dengue research section with the paper’s exact figures, tables, limitations and a complete study view · AI & Digital Innovation studio with honestly labelled experience levels · projects gallery of verified work only · interactive Knowledge Universe map · mailto contact form · LinkedIn and X links · custom 404 view for unknown in-page routes · back-to-top control.

Testing performed on this build: a full-project text search confirms the excluded score terms and private personal details appear nowhere — homepage, hidden content, metadata and the downloadable résumé included; school name verified as Buner Public School Jangai; every button, dialog, quiz, clock and canvas is wired to real code in this file; layout checked at desktop and phone widths with no horizontal overflow; keyboard focus, skip link, aria labels and reduced-motion fallbacks included throughout. The Knowledge Engine loads Three.js from CDN and degrades to a written fallback if WebGL or the network is unavailable.

The Complete Study

AbstractIntroductionMethodsResultsDiscussionConclusionLimitationsDeclarationsReferencesAuthor Queries

Demographic, clinical and serological profile of dengue patients admitted to Mardan Medical Complex, Pakistan, October 2019 – January 2020

Shah Fahad, Muhammad Ayaz Khan — Department of Biochemistry, Faculty of Chemical and Life Sciences, Abdul Wali Khan University Mardan, Pakistan. Supervisor: Dr. Sulaiman, Associate Professor.

Status: original research manuscript. It has not been published in, or accepted by, any journal, and is presented here as the authors' study record.

Abstract

Background. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease spread by Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus. Hospital-based data from district Mardan are scarce.

Methods. We interviewed admitted, laboratory-confirmed dengue patients at Mardan Medical Complex (MMC) face to face with a 23-item questionnaire between October 2019 and January 2020. Infection was confirmed by immunochromatographic test (ICT) for NS1 antigen, IgG and IgM. Data were analysed descriptively in Microsoft Excel.

Findings. We included 153 patients: 111 men (72.5%) and 42 women (27.5%). Most were aged 15–30 years (n=63) or 45–70 years (n=44). Unemployed people (34%) and labourers (25%) predominated, and 69.9% were married. Cases peaked in October (53%). All patients had fever and headache. All were NS1 positive; 86 were also IgG positive, 29 IgM positive and 38 positive for both. About 44% knew that mosquito bites transmit dengue.

Interpretation. Admitted dengue patients were mainly young and middle-aged men, with a clear post-monsoon peak and low awareness of transmission. Education and vector control should start before autumn.

Keywords: dengue; Mardan; Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; NS1; IgG; IgM; awareness

Key points. Of 153 admitted dengue patients, almost three in four were men (72.5%). Cases peaked in October (53%) and fell to 9% by January. Only about 44% of patients knew that mosquitoes transmit dengue. Unemployed people and labourers made up roughly 60% of cases.

1 · Introduction

Dengue is caused by dengue virus, which has four serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4). It is transmitted mainly by female Aedes aegypti, with Ae. albopictus as a secondary vector, and is most common in tropical and subtropical urban areas. Illness ranges from classical dengue fever to dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF) and dengue shock syndrome (DSS), the most severe form (Gubler, 1998). There is no specific antiviral treatment; care is supportive, with fluids and monitoring of platelet count and haematocrit (WHO, 1997). Prevention therefore depends on vector control and on limiting human–mosquito contact.

Pakistan has had recurrent dengue outbreaks, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has been affected in recent years. Mardan, the province's second largest city, has reported dengue since 2013, and its hot, humid climate favours mosquito breeding. Local clinical and serological data remain limited.

We aimed to describe dengue cases by sex, age, occupation and marital status; to record symptoms and serology; to describe the monthly pattern; and to assess patients' knowledge of transmission.

2 · Methods

Design and setting. A hospital-based descriptive survey was done at MMC, district Mardan (population about 2.78 million in 2018), from October 2019 to January 2020.

Participants. Men and women with dengue who were admitted to MMC were included. Patients not admitted to MMC were excluded.

Data collection. Hospital permission was obtained, and doctors and laboratory staff assisted. A 23-item English questionnaire, mostly multiple choice, was built from published Pakistani dengue studies and approved by the supervisor. It covered background, symptoms, laboratory results and knowledge of dengue.

Laboratory tests and analysis. ICT detected NS1 antigen, IgG and IgM. Data were summarised as counts and percentages in Microsoft Excel 2007.

3 · Results

Who was affected. 153 patients: 111 men (72.5%) and 42 women (27.5%) — men outnumbered women by about 2.6 to 1. By age group: 0–15 years, 19 patients; 15–30, 63; 30–45, 24; 45–70, 44. The age groups sum to 150, so age was missing for three patients. By occupation: unemployed 52, labourers 38, students 21, children under 10, 19, government employees 16, own business 7. Unemployed people and labourers accounted for 59% of cases. Married patients numbered 107 (69.9%) and unmarried 46 (30.1%).

Presentation and timing. Presenting symptoms (% of patients): fever 100%, headache 100%, body aching 70%, abdominal pain 60%, vomiting 40%, skin rash 20%. Share of cases by month: October 53%, November 28%, December 11%, January 9% — cases fell steadily as temperatures dropped. (The monthly percentages as reported sum to 101%, a rounding artefact in the original.)

Serology. All 153 patients were NS1 positive. ICT patterns: 86 patients NS1+/IgG+/IgM− (56.2%); 29 patients NS1+/IgG−/IgM+ (19.0%); 38 patients NS1+/IgG+/IgM+ (24.8%).

Knowledge of transmission. Asked how dengue is transmitted, patients answered: mosquito bite 68, waterborne 33, airborne 28, don't know 23 — the recorded answers sum to 152, so one response is not accounted for in the original paper. Many also did not know when mosquitoes bite, and some used other medicines before coming to hospital.

All figures and the serology table are displayed in the Research section of this page (Figures 1–7, Table 1).

4 · Discussion

This study describes 153 patients admitted with dengue to a tertiary hospital in Mardan in the 2019 post-monsoon season. About three-quarters were men. This may reflect greater outdoor and occupational exposure, or unequal access to hospital care. Because only admitted patients were studied, we cannot say that dengue was truly more frequent in men.

Cases clustered in young adults, with a second group aged 45 years and over. Unemployed people and labourers made up about 60% of patients. We observed that labourers were mostly infected at work rather than at home, which fits the daytime biting habit of Aedes; we did not test this formally.

Fever, headache, body aching and abdominal pain are typical of dengue but overlap with other fevers, so laboratory confirmation matters. All patients were NS1 positive; those with IgG, alone or with IgM, may have had secondary infection, which carries a higher risk of severe disease. An ICT result cannot confirm this, and serotyping was not done.

The steady fall in cases from October to January matches cooling weather and declining mosquito activity. Only about 44% of patients knew the mosquito route, and we noted that women and older people knew less. Late presentation and self-medication, mostly among labourers, are a further concern.

5 · Conclusion

Admitted dengue patients at MMC were mainly young and middle-aged men, with an October peak and poor knowledge of transmission. We recommend awareness campaigns before the post-monsoon season, especially for women and older people; removal of standing water; repellents and nets; and early consultation for fever during outbreaks. Larger multi-centre studies with serotyping and severity data are needed.

Limitations

  • Single-centre study at one hospital over four months.
  • Hospital-based sample of admitted, ICT-confirmed patients only — no population denominator, so incidence and prevalence cannot be calculated.
  • Age information missing for three of the 153 patients; one transmission-awareness response unaccounted for.
  • Severity grading, platelet counts and dengue serotypes were not reported.
  • Descriptive analysis only; no inferential statistics were used, and no significance claims are made.

Declarations

Ethics: hospital permission was obtained; institutional ethics approval details are not stated in the paper — to be confirmed by the author. Conflicts of interest and funding: not stated in the paper — to be completed by the authors. Acknowledgements: Dr. Sulaiman, and the doctors and laboratory staff of Mardan Medical Complex.

References

  • Gubler DJ. Dengue and dengue hemorrhagic fever. Clinical Microbiology Reviews 1998.
  • World Health Organization. Dengue haemorrhagic fever: diagnosis, treatment, prevention and control. 2nd edition. Geneva: WHO; 1997.

Further sources from the thesis literature review are to be added only after checking them against the originals.

Author Queries — items requiring confirmation

  • Institutional ethics approval details (committee and reference), if any.
  • Funding source and conflicts of interest declarations.
  • Underlying monthly case counts (the paper reports monthly percentages only).
  • How the three missing age values and the one unaccounted awareness response were handled.
  • ICT kit manufacturer and any quality-control procedures, if to be reported.
